tool.name: Elasticsearch
tool.tagline: Distributed search and analytics engine for full-text, logs and vectors
tool.description: Elasticsearch is a distributed search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene. You index JSON documents and query them over a REST API with relevance-ranked full-text search, filters, aggregations and vector search. It powers site search, log and metrics analytics (the Elastic Stack) and retrieval for AI applications.

glossary.def: In Elasticsearch: a named collection of JSON documents, roughly like a table. Indexing a document means storing it there so it can be searched.
In Elasticsearch: one JSON record stored in an index and identified by its _id, roughly like a row in a table.
One running Elasticsearch server. Several nodes working together form a cluster and share the index's shards.
In Elasticsearch: splitting an index into pieces (shards) spread over the nodes. Each primary shard holds part of the documents; replica shards are copies of it.
Elastic's web app for exploring Elasticsearch data, with dashboards and a Dev Tools console for sending requests.
Searchable shortly after being written (in Elasticsearch, by default within about a second) rather than instantly.
The Elasticsearch step that makes recently written documents visible to search, by default about once a second.
Elasticsearch guessing a field's type from the first value it sees, when no mapping defines it.
Avoiding lost updates without locks: you send the version you last read along with your change, and the write is refused if someone changed the data since.
One document that matched a search, returned with its relevance score.
In Elasticsearch: one searchable unit made from text, usually a lower-cased word. Searches look up terms, not raw text.
The number (_score) Elasticsearch gives each hit for how well it matches the query; hits are sorted by it, best first.
A multiplier that makes matches in one field or clause count more (or less) toward the relevance score, e.g. name^3.
The schema of an Elasticsearch index: each field's type and how it is stored for searching.
Turning text into searchable terms: cleaning it, cutting it into words, lower-casing and similar steps, done both when storing and when searching.
In Elasticsearch: a field type that stores a string as one exact value, for filters, sorting and aggregations, rather than cutting it into words.
One value stored in two ways under one field, typically as text for full-text search plus a keyword copy for exact matching and sorting.
An index collecting a huge number of different fields, often from uncontrolled dynamic mapping, which slows the whole cluster.
Copying documents from one Elasticsearch index into another (usually with a new mapping), so they are stored and analyzed again.
An Elasticsearch query that looks up exact values without analyzing the input: term, terms, range, exists and similar.
Elasticsearch's notation for relative dates, like now-7d/d: seven days ago, rounded down to the start of that day.
The Elasticsearch query that combines others with must, should, filter and must_not clauses.
Parts of an Elasticsearch query that ask "how well does it match?" and add to the relevance score.
Parts of an Elasticsearch query that only ask "does it match?": no scoring, so they are faster and can be cached.
The Elasticsearch component that turns text into terms: character filters, then a tokenizer, then token filters.
In Elasticsearch text analysis: the step that splits text into tokens, usually words.
In Elasticsearch text analysis: one piece of text, usually a word, cut out by the tokenizer before token filters turn it into a term.
A very common word such as "the" or "and" that text search often drops because it says little about what a text is about.
Cutting words down to a common root, so running, runs and run all become run and match each other in searches.
A light clean-up, such as lower-casing, applied to an Elasticsearch keyword field while keeping the value as one term.
The standard formula search engines use to score text matches, from how often the words appear, how rare they are and how long the field is.
How often a search term appears in a field; more often scores higher, with diminishing returns.
A measure of how rare a term is across all documents; rare terms count more in the relevance score.
Merging several ranked result lists by each document's position in them, rather than by their scores, which may not be comparable.
An Elasticsearch aggregation that computes a number from documents, such as avg, sum, max or percentiles.
An Elasticsearch aggregation that sorts documents into groups (buckets), such as one per status value or one per day.
An Elasticsearch aggregation computed from other aggregations' results, such as a running total.
A column-by-column copy of field values on disk that Elasticsearch uses for sorting and aggregations; keyword, number and date fields have it.
A filter shown beside search results with a count for each choice, like "Brand: Acme (12)".
An Elasticsearch view of an index frozen at one moment, so paging through results sees the same data even while it changes.
A set of Lucene index files inside a shard that is never changed once written; new writes create new segments, which are later merged.
Elasticsearch Query Language: queries written as steps joined by |, such as FROM logs | WHERE ... | STATS ..., producing a table.
Elasticsearch's JSON query format, the { "query": { "match": ... } } style, built for relevance-ranked search.
In Elasticsearch: the rule that picks which shard a document goes to, by default from a hash of its _id.
Elasticsearch's traffic-light summary of shard placement: green (all placed), yellow (some replicas missing), red (some primary missing).
An Elasticsearch node allowed to manage the cluster's shared state, such as which shard is on which node. Three are typical, so one can fail.
A series of steps Elasticsearch applies to documents before storing them, such as parsing a date or removing a field.
An Elasticsearch field type that stores each object of a list as a hidden document of its own, so each object's fields stay together in searches.
In Elasticsearch: a second name pointing at one or more indices, so applications can switch indices without changing code.
Elasticsearch settings and mappings applied automatically to every new index whose name matches a pattern.
Hierarchical navigable small world: a graph linking each vector to its near neighbours, used to find close vectors quickly but approximately.
k nearest neighbours: finding the k stored vectors closest to a query vector.
Storing numbers with fewer bits (for example 8 bits instead of 32) to save memory, at a small cost in accuracy.
An Elasticsearch connection to a machine learning model (built in or from an outside service) that it calls to create embeddings or other results.
Combining word-based (BM25) and vector search results into one list, usually with reciprocal rank fusion.
An Elasticsearch building block that produces a ranked result list (a normal query, a kNN search, or a fusion of others).
The core search structure: for each term, the list of documents (and positions) that contain it, like the index at the back of a book.
Elasticsearch's per-shard log of recent writes, saved to disk before a write is confirmed and replayed after a crash.
In Elasticsearch: a Lucene commit that saves segments permanently to disk and trims the translog.
Lucene combining small segments into bigger ones in the background, dropping deleted documents to reclaim space.
The open-source search library inside Elasticsearch; each shard is one Lucene index.
The Elasticsearch node that receives a request, sends it on to the shards involved, and merges their answers.
The first step of an Elasticsearch search: each shard finds its own top hits and returns just their ids and scores.
The second step of an Elasticsearch search: the coordinating node gets the full documents for the overall winners only.
An Elasticsearch name for append-only, time-stamped data that writes to the newest of a series of hidden indices and searches all of them.
One of the hidden indices behind an Elasticsearch data stream, each holding one stretch of time.
Starting a new index for writes once the current one reaches a set size, age or document count.
Index lifecycle management: Elasticsearch policies that move indices through phases (hot, warm, cold) and delete them after a set age.
A simpler alternative to ILM for data streams that only sets how long data is kept, handling rollover automatically.

concepts.name: Indices, documents and the REST API
concepts.summary: Elasticsearch stores JSON documents in indices and lets you search them by sending it web requests (a REST API).
concepts.why: Knowing the core words and the request style lets you read any Elasticsearch example.
concepts.body:
A SQL database is great at exact questions such as "orders with status 'paid'". It's poor at the searching people do in a search box: finding "blue pens" in product names, forgiving typos, and putting the best matches first. That kind of searching is **full-text search**, and it's what **Elasticsearch** is built for.

Elasticsearch stores data as **JSON**, a common text format for records: `{"name": "Blue pen", "price": 1.5}`. Each `"name": value` pair is a **field**, much like one column's value in a row.

One JSON record stored in Elasticsearch is a **document**, identified by an `_id`. Documents live in an **index**, which is roughly a table. (That's a different meaning from the SQL index you know, although Elasticsearch does build lookup structures for every field so it can search them.) The original JSON is kept in `_source`.

Elasticsearch can spread one index over several servers. Each running Elasticsearch server is a **node**, and nodes working together form a **cluster**. An index is split into pieces called **shards**, which are spread over the nodes; you never deal with shards directly.

You talk to Elasticsearch over **HTTP**, the same system websites are reached with. Each **request** names an action, such as `GET` (read), `PUT` (store), `POST` (send data to act on) or `DELETE`; then a path saying what to act on; and often some JSON. A design like this, with paths for things and HTTP actions for what to do with them, is a **REST API**.

- `PUT /products` creates an index, `DELETE /products` removes it,
- `PUT /products/_doc/1` stores a document, `GET /products/_doc/1` fetches it,
- `GET /products/_search` searches, `GET /_cluster/health` checks the cluster.

Examples, here and in Elastic's documentation, use the format of the Dev Tools console in **Kibana**, Elastic's companion app for exploring data: the action and path on one line, then any JSON. The same requests work from the `curl` command or from your own code.

Elasticsearch is **near real-time**: a new document shows up in searches after the next **refresh**, by default within about a second, though fetching it by `_id` works straight away. It has no transactions across several documents, so it usually holds a searchable copy of data whose main copy lives in another database.
concepts.code:
# check the cluster
GET /_cluster/health
# { "cluster_name": "docker-cluster", "status": "green", "number_of_nodes": 1, ... }

# create an empty index called products
PUT /products

# list indices: pri = primary shards, rep = copies of each
GET /_cat/indices?v&h=health,status,index,pri,rep,docs.count
# health status index    pri rep docs.count
# yellow open   products   1   1          0

# the same health check from a terminal with curl
# curl -u elastic:$ES_PASSWORD https://localhost:9200/_cluster/health?pretty
takeaways: Index = collection of JSON documents; each has an _id and _source
Everything is an HTTP request, usually with a JSON body
Indices are split into shards spread over nodes
Near real-time: searchable after a refresh (about 1 s)
pitfalls: Using Elasticsearch as the only copy of important data that needs transactions.

quiz.q: You index a document and immediately search for it, but it is not found; a second later it is. Why?
options: Search sees documents only after a refresh, about every second
Search requires an explicit commit call
quiz.explain: Elasticsearch is near real-time: new documents become searchable at the next refresh.

concepts.name: Indexing, getting and updating documents
concepts.summary: Create, read, update and delete single documents, and understand versions and automatically generated ids.
concepts.why: Every search starts with getting documents in, and these requests are the building blocks for keeping Elasticsearch in step with your main database.
concepts.body:
`PUT /index/_doc/<id>` creates the document with that id, or **replaces** it entirely if it exists. `POST /index/_doc` (no id) lets Elasticsearch make up an id. `PUT /index/_create/<id>` refuses with error 409 if the id already exists, so sending it twice can't overwrite anything: it's **idempotent**, safe to repeat.

If the index doesn't exist yet, it's created with default settings, and **dynamic mapping** guesses each field's type from the first values it sees (a later lesson covers this).

`GET /index/_doc/<id>` returns the document's `_source` plus some bookkeeping fields: `_version`, `_seq_no` and `_primary_term`. Unlike search, fetching by id always sees the latest write.

Elasticsearch never edits a stored document in place, so an "update" really writes a new copy. `POST /index/_update/<id>` with `{ "doc": { ... } }` merges the given fields into the stored source and saves a new version. You can also update with a **script**, a short snippet of code run on the document (`ctx._source.stock -= params.n` subtracts n from stock), or use `doc_as_upsert` to create the document if it's missing (an **upsert**). `DELETE /index/_doc/<id>` removes one document.

Two programs may change the same document at once, and one could silently overwrite the other's change. **Optimistic concurrency control** prevents that without locks: read `_seq_no` and `_primary_term`, then write with `?if_seq_no=..&if_primary_term=..`. If someone changed the document in the meantime, you get a 409 conflict and can re-read and try again.

In tests, add `?refresh=wait_for` when the change must be searchable before the call returns. Avoid it in code that writes a lot, because it slows every write down.
takeaways: PUT with an id creates or replaces; POST without an id generates one
_update merges a partial document or runs a script, creating a new version
GET by id is real-time; search waits for refresh
if_seq_no + if_primary_term give optimistic concurrency control
pitfalls: Using PUT /index/_doc/id with partial fields and wiping the rest: PUT replaces the whole document.

quiz.q: What does PUT /products/_doc/1 with body { "price": 2 } do to an existing document with name and price?
options: Replaces the document, so name is gone
Appends a second document with id 1
quiz.explain: PUT replaces the whole source; use _update for partial changes.

concepts.name: Search basics and the match query
concepts.summary: Run _search with a match query, read the hits and their scores, and control which fields come back.
concepts.why: Searching text and putting the best matches first is the reason Elasticsearch exists.
concepts.body:
`GET /index/_search` with a `query` returns the matching documents, called **hits**, best first. The workhorse query for text is **match**: `{ "match": { "name": "blue pens" } }`.

Elasticsearch first cuts the query text into **terms**, roughly lower-cased words (`blue`, `pens`), the same way it cut up the stored text, then finds documents containing any of them. Each hit gets a **relevance score** (`_score`): documents with more of the terms, and with rarer ones, score higher.

The **response**, the JSON Elasticsearch sends back, contains:

- `hits.total`: the number of matches (counted exactly up to 10,000 by default; above that it says "at least", with `"relation": "gte"`),
- `hits.hits`: the top results, each with `_id`, `_score` and `_source`,
- `took` (milliseconds the search took) and `timed_out`.

Useful options on `match`: `"operator": "and"` to require every term, `"fuzziness": "AUTO"` to forgive small typos, and `minimum_should_match` for rules like "at least 2 of 3 words". `multi_match` searches several fields at once, e.g. `["name^3", "description"]`, where `^3` makes name matches count three times as much (a **boost**).

Shape the response with `size` (how many hits, default 10), `_source` filtering (`"_source": ["name", "price"]`, only these fields) and `highlight`, which returns the matching snippets with the matched words wrapped in `<em>` tags, ready to show in bold.

A search with no query, or `{ "match_all": {} }`, returns everything, each with score 1.0. `GET /index/_count` returns just the number of matches.
takeaways: match cuts the query into terms and ranks hits by relevance (_score)
operator: and, fuzziness and minimum_should_match tune matching
multi_match with ^boost searches several fields
size, _source filtering and highlight shape the response
pitfalls: Reading hits.total as exact for big result sets: beyond 10,000 it only means "at least", unless track_total_hits is true.

quiz.q: A match query for "red shoes" uses the default operator. Which documents match?
options: Those containing red or shoes, ranked by relevance
None, because match needs a single word
quiz.explain: The default operator is or; documents with more matching terms score higher.

concepts.name: Mappings: text vs keyword
concepts.summary: Define field types explicitly, especially text for full-text search versus keyword for exact values, sorting and aggregations.
concepts.why: Most Elasticsearch mistakes and slow queries trace back to a field stored as the wrong type.
concepts.body:
A **mapping** is the schema of an index: each field's type and how it's stored for searching. If you don't define one, **dynamic mapping** guesses from the first document it sees: numbers become `long` or `float`, strings that look like dates (`2026-10-17`) become `date`, and every other string becomes a `text` field with a `.keyword` subfield.

The crucial choice is between the two string types:

- **text** is **analyzed**: cut into separate lower-cased words, called terms, for full-text search ("Blue Pen" becomes `blue` and `pen`). You can't sort or aggregate on it efficiently.
- **keyword** stores the exact value as one single term, for filters, sorting, aggregations and ids ("SKU-001", "paid", email addresses).

Other common types: `integer`, `long`, `float`, `scaled_float`, `double`, `date`, `boolean`, `ip`, `geo_point` (a place on a map), `object`, `nested` and `dense_vector`. A **multi-field** stores one value both ways: `"fields": { "raw": { "type": "keyword" } }` adds an exact `raw` copy next to the text field.

Define mappings explicitly for real, long-lived indices: `PUT /index { "mappings": { "properties": {...} } }`. Set `"dynamic": "strict"` to reject unknown fields, or `false` to store them without making them searchable. Letting new fields appear freely can lead to a **mapping explosion**: thousands of fields slowing the cluster (the default limit is 1,000 fields).

You can add new fields to an existing mapping, but you **cannot change** an existing field's type; that requires creating a new index and copying the data into it (reindexing).
takeaways: text = analyzed for full-text search; keyword = exact value for filters, sorts and aggregations
Dynamic mapping makes strings text + .keyword
Define mappings explicitly for real indices; consider dynamic: strict
Existing field types can't change: reindex instead
pitfalls: Mapping ids, statuses or emails as text, and then wondering why exact filters and aggregations misbehave.

quiz.q: You need to sort products by brand name and also search brand with typos. How should brand be mapped?
quiz.explain: A multi-field gives full-text search on text and sorting/aggregation on the keyword subfield.

concepts.name: Exact values: term, terms and range
concepts.summary: Filter on exact keyword values, numbers and dates with term, terms, range and exists queries.
concepts.why: Filters like a status, a price range or a date window are part of almost every real search request.
concepts.body:
**Term-level queries** look up exact values without analyzing the input:

- `term`: one exact value, `{ "term": { "status": "paid" } }`,
- `terms`: any of several values, `{ "terms": { "status": ["paid", "shipped"] } }`,
- `range`: numbers, dates or strings with `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`,
- `exists`: the field has an indexed value; `prefix`, `wildcard` and `ids` also exist.

Use them on `keyword`, numeric, date and boolean fields. Using `term` on a **text** field is the classic mistake: the stored terms are analyzed (lower-cased, split), so `{ "term": { "name": "Blue pen" } }` matches nothing, while `match` would. If you need the exact original string, query the `.keyword` subfield.

Date ranges accept **date math**: `"gte": "now-7d/d"` means seven days ago rounded down to the start of the day, and `"lt": "now/d"` is the start of today. Rounding means the same filter text repeats exactly all day, so Elasticsearch can reuse its earlier answer from a **cache** (a store of recent results). Add `"format"` or `"time_zone"` when your dates aren't in the standard `2026-10-17T09:00:00Z` form, in UTC.

Exact filters don't need scoring. Put them in the `filter` clause of a `bool` query (next lesson) so Elasticsearch skips scoring and can cache the result, which is both faster and more correct than letting a filter affect relevance.
takeaways: term, terms, range and exists match exact values without analysis
Use them on keyword, numeric, date and boolean fields
term on a text field usually finds nothing; use match or .keyword
Rounded date math like now-7d/d lets results be cached
pitfalls: Querying a text field with term and getting zero results.

quiz.q: A status field is mapped as text. Why might { "term": { "status": "Shipped" } } return nothing?
options: The indexed terms were lower-cased to shipped, and term doesn't analyze the input
term is not supported on text
Status values are stored in _source only
quiz.explain: Text fields store analyzed terms; term looks up the input exactly as given.

concepts.name: Combining queries with bool
concepts.summary: Combine full-text and exact conditions with must, should, filter and must_not, and know which affect scoring.
concepts.why: Real search boxes mix text relevance with filters, boosts and exclusions, all expressed through bool.
concepts.body:
The **bool** query combines clauses:

- `must`: must match and **contributes to the score**,
- `filter`: must match, **no scoring**, cacheable,
- `should`: optional matches that raise the score; if there is no `must` or `filter`, at least one `should` must match (`minimum_should_match` controls this),
- `must_not`: excludes matches, runs in filter context.

A typical product search puts the user's text in `must` (a `match` or `multi_match`), structured conditions like category, price range and in-stock in `filter`, preferences in `should` (boost items on sale or from a favourite brand), and exclusions such as discontinued items in `must_not`.

This split between **query context** (how well does it match?) and **filter context** (does it match at all?) is central. Filters are faster, are kept in each node's cache when used repeatedly, and don't distort relevance.

Bool queries nest, so you can express `(A or B) and not C` by putting a bool with two `should` clauses inside a `filter`. Use `"boost"` on individual clauses to weigh them. To see why a document got its score, add `"explain": true` to the request, or use `GET /index/_explain/<id>`.
takeaways: must and should score; filter and must_not don't
Put exact conditions in filter for speed, caching and clean relevance
should boosts optional preferences
bool queries nest to build any logic
pitfalls: Putting exact filters in must, so they inflate scores and can't be cached as filters.

quiz.q: Which clause should hold a price range that must apply but shouldn't affect ranking?
quiz.explain: filter requires the match without contributing to the score.

quiz.q: A bool query has only should clauses and no must or filter. What is required to match?
quiz.explain: Without must or filter, minimum_should_match defaults to 1.

concepts.name: Text analysis and analyzers
concepts.summary: See how analyzers turn text into terms with character filters, a tokenizer and token filters, and build your own.
concepts.why: Whether a search finds 'running' for 'run' or 'café' for 'cafe' is decided by analysis.
concepts.body:
When a `text` field is stored, an **analyzer** turns it into terms in three steps:

- **character filters** clean the raw text (strip HTML formatting, replace characters),
- a **tokenizer** splits it into **tokens**, usually words (`standard` splits at word boundaries for any language's alphabet, `whitespace` at spaces, `keyword` keeps the whole text as one token),
- **token filters** transform the tokens: `lowercase`; `asciifolding` (café to cafe); `stop`, which drops very common **stop words** like "the"; `stemmer`, which cuts words to their root (**stemming**: running to run); `synonym_graph`, which treats listed words as equal; and `edge_ngram`, which also stores each word's beginnings (b, bl, blu, blue) for search-as-you-type.

The default `standard` analyzer is the standard tokenizer plus lowercase. Language analyzers like `english` add stop words and stemming.

The same analysis normally runs on the **query** text too, which is why `match` works. You can set a different `search_analyzer`: for example, store with `edge_ngram` for search-as-you-type but search with `standard`, so the query text isn't cut into beginnings as well.

`POST /index/_analyze` shows exactly which terms an analyzer produces, and it's the first tool to reach for when a search mysteriously doesn't match.

Analyzers are defined in the index **settings** and used from the mapping. Changing an analyzer for existing data requires reindexing, since the terms were computed when the documents were stored. For keyword fields, a **normalizer** (e.g. lowercase) applies a light clean-up while keeping the value as one term.
takeaways: Analyzer = character filters + tokenizer + token filters
Query text is analyzed with the same (or a search_) analyzer
_analyze shows the exact terms produced
Changing analysis means reindexing
pitfalls: Adding synonyms or stemming to the mapping of an existing index and expecting old documents to match differently without reindexing.

quiz.q: Documents contain "running" but a match query for "run" finds nothing. What is the likely fix?
options: Use an analyzer with a stemmer, then reindex
quiz.explain: Stemming reduces both running and run to the same term, but existing data must be reindexed.

concepts.name: Relevance scoring and tuning
concepts.summary: Understand BM25 scoring, and tune relevance with field boosts, phrase matching, function_score and explain.
concepts.why: Users judge search by whether the best result is first, which takes deliberate relevance tuning.
concepts.body:
Elasticsearch scores text matches with a formula called **BM25** by default. For each query term in each field, the score grows with:

- **term frequency** (TF): how often the term occurs in the field (with diminishing returns, controlled by `k1`),
- **inverse document frequency** (IDF): terms that are rare across the index count more,
- shorter fields: a match in a short title beats one in a long body (length normalization, controlled by `b`).

Scores are relative, comparable only within one query, so never apply fixed score thresholds across queries.

Tuning tools, roughly in the order to try them:

- **field boosts** in `multi_match` (`"title^3"`), and `type: "best_fields"`, `"most_fields"` or `"cross_fields"` depending on how fields relate,
- **phrase proximity**: add a `match_phrase` with `slop` in `should` to reward words appearing together,
- **business signals** with `function_score` or `script_score`: blend popularity, recency (`gauss` decay on a date) or rating into the score; `rank_feature` fields are an efficient alternative,
- **synonyms** at search time.

Use `"explain": true` to see each document's score breakdown, and test changes against a set of real queries whose right answers people have marked (the `_rank_eval` request) rather than eyeballing one query.

Hybrid search, which mixes this word matching with search by meaning (the vector search lesson), produces two kinds of scores that can't be compared. Combine the two result lists with **reciprocal rank fusion** (RRF), which merges them by position in each list instead.
takeaways: BM25: term frequency, rarity (IDF) and field length drive scores
Scores are relative to a query; don't threshold them
Boost fields, reward phrases, then blend business signals
Measure changes with judged queries, not single examples
pitfalls: Tuning boosts based on one query and making ten others worse.

quiz.q: All else equal, which document scores higher for the term "zephyr" under BM25?
options: One where zephyr appears once in a 5,000-word body
One where zephyr appears once in a 5-word title
quiz.explain: Length normalization gives a match in a short field more weight.

concepts.name: Aggregations
concepts.summary: Compute facets, statistics and counts per period with terms, metric and date_histogram aggregations, and nest them inside each other.
concepts.why: Faceted navigation, dashboards and log analytics are all aggregations over search results.
concepts.body:
**Aggregations** summarise the documents matched by the query, in the same request, much like SQL's GROUP BY and aggregate functions. Set `"size": 0` when you only want the summary, not the hits.

- **Metric** aggregations compute numbers: `avg`, `sum`, `min`, `max`, `stats`, `percentiles`, and `cardinality` (an approximate count of distinct values, cheap even for millions).
- **Bucket** aggregations sort documents into groups: `terms` (the top values of a keyword field), `range`, `histogram` (counts per fixed-size range of numbers), `date_histogram` (per day with `calendar_interval: "day"`, or every 5 minutes with `fixed_interval: "5m"`) and `filters`.
- **Sub-aggregations** nest inside buckets: average price per category, errors per server per hour.
- **Pipeline** aggregations work on other aggregations' results: `derivative`, `cumulative_sum`, `bucket_sort`.

Aggregations read **doc values**: a column-by-column copy on disk that `keyword`, numeric and date fields have by default. That's why you aggregate on `category` (keyword) or `category.keyword`, not on a `text` field, which gives an error by default.

Know the approximations: `terms` collects the top values from each shard and merges them, so counts can be slightly off with many shards (`doc_count_error_upper_bound` says by how much, and `shard_size` trades extra work for accuracy). `cardinality` is approximate, tunable with `precision_threshold`. To page through every combination of buckets, use the `composite` aggregation instead of a huge `terms` size.

The filter counts beside shop search results, like "Brand: Acme (12)", are **facets**. They're typically one `terms` aggregation per attribute, with the shopper's choices applied through `post_filter` (a filter applied to the hits but not to the aggregations), so the facets still show the other options.
takeaways: Metric aggregations compute values; bucket aggregations group; sub-aggregations nest
size: 0 when you only want aggregations
Aggregate on keyword, numeric and date fields (doc values), not text
terms and cardinality are approximate across shards
pitfalls: Running a terms aggregation with size: 100000 to list everything; use composite and page through it.

quiz.q: Why does a terms aggregation on a text field like description fail by default?
options: Text fields have no doc values, and the slower alternative (fielddata) is turned off
quiz.explain: Aggregations read doc values; text fields don't have them, so use a keyword field.

concepts.name: Sorting and deep pagination
concepts.summary: Sort results by fields and page through them with from/size for shallow pages and search_after with a point in time for deep ones.
concepts.why: Result lists need stable ordering and paging, and naive deep paging hits hard limits.
concepts.body:
By default hits are ordered by `_score`. `"sort": [{ "price": "asc" }, { "_score": "desc" }]` sorts by fields; sort on keyword, numeric or date fields, never on analyzed text.

**from/size** paging (`"from": 20, "size": 10` for page 3) is fine for the first pages. Each shard must produce `from + size` hits, and the node handling the request merges them all, so cost grows with depth, and requests beyond `index.max_result_window` (10,000 by default) are rejected.

For deep pagination or exporting results use **search_after**:

- open a **point in time** (PIT, `POST /index/_pit?keep_alive=1m`): a frozen view of the index, so every page sees the same data even while documents change,
- sort by your fields plus the implicit `_shard_doc` tie-breaker that PIT searches add,
- pass each last hit's `sort` values as `search_after` in the next request,
- close the PIT when done.

`search_after` can't jump to page 500 directly, which matches how infinite scroll and exports work anyway. The older **scroll** request still exists but is no longer recommended for deep pagination; prefer PIT with search_after.

`track_total_hits` controls exact counting: `false` skips it entirely for speed, `true` counts exactly at a cost.
takeaways: Sort on keyword, numeric or date fields
from/size for shallow pages; limited to 10,000 by default
Deep paging: point in time + search_after
Close PITs when you're done
pitfalls: Raising max_result_window to millions to keep using from/size, which loads the cluster heavily.

quiz.q: An export job must read all 3 million matching documents consistently. What should it use?
options: A point in time with search_after
quiz.explain: PIT gives a consistent snapshot and search_after pages efficiently at any depth.

concepts.name: Bulk indexing and refresh
concepts.summary: Load and change many documents efficiently with _bulk, update_by_query and refresh settings.
concepts.why: Syncing data from a database or another system needs fast indexing without swamping the cluster.
concepts.body:
Sending one document per request wastes time on the back-and-forth: every **round trip** adds delay. The **_bulk** request carries many actions at once, written as NDJSON, also called **JSON Lines**: one JSON object per line. Each action line (`index`, `create`, `update` or `delete`) is followed, except for delete, by a line with the document. The body must end with a line break.

The response says `"errors": true` if any item failed, and gives a status per item, so always check it: a bulk request can partly succeed. Elastic's libraries for each programming language include bulk helpers that split the work into chunks, send them at the same time and report failures.

Tips for speed:

- requests of roughly 5 to 15 MB each; measure rather than guess,
- several senders working in parallel, slowing down when they get status `429`, which means the node's queue of waiting writes is full,
- for big first loads, set `"refresh_interval": "-1"` and `"number_of_replicas": 0`, then restore both afterwards,
- let Elasticsearch generate ids when you don't need your own; it saves a lookup.

Each refresh makes recent writes searchable by creating a new **segment**, a small set of index files, so frequent refreshes cost processor time and disk work. The default `1s` (applied only while the index is being searched) is a good balance; `?refresh=wait_for` on a request waits for the next refresh.

To change documents already in the index as a set, use `_update_by_query` and `_delete_by_query` with a query and, for updates, a script. They run as background tasks, can be slowed down on purpose (throttled) so they don't swamp the cluster, and report version conflicts.
takeaways: _bulk sends many actions as NDJSON, ending with a line break
Check errors and per-item status: bulk can partly succeed
Turn off refresh and replicas during big first loads
update_by_query and delete_by_query change sets of documents
pitfalls: Ignoring the bulk response and silently losing documents that were rejected because they didn't fit the mapping.

quiz.q: A bulk request returns HTTP 200 with "errors": true. What does that mean?
options: Some items failed; check each item's status
quiz.explain: Bulk is not atomic: the HTTP call succeeded but individual items may have failed.

concepts.name: ES|QL piped queries
concepts.summary: Query, filter, transform and aggregate data with ES|QL, a language of steps joined by |, sent with POST /_query.
concepts.why: ES|QL makes analysis and log exploration readable, without deeply nested JSON.
concepts.body:
**ES|QL** (Elasticsearch Query Language) is written as a chain of steps: a source command, then processing commands separated by `|`. Each step takes the table of results from the previous step and transforms it, like an assembly line.

- `FROM logs-*` picks indices, data streams or aliases (`*` matches any characters),
- `WHERE status >= 500 AND host LIKE "web-*"` filters,
- `EVAL ms = duration / 1000000` computes columns, `KEEP` and `DROP` choose them, `RENAME` renames,
- `STATS errors = COUNT(*), p95 = PERCENTILE(latency, 95) BY host` aggregates,
- `SORT errors DESC | LIMIT 10` orders and limits,
- `DISSECT` and `GROK` pull fields out of text while the query runs, `ENRICH` adds fields from another index, and `LOOKUP JOIN` joins with a lookup index.

Send it with `POST /_query` and a `"query"` string; add `?format=txt` or `csv` to get a plain table back. Kibana's Discover page runs ES|QL directly.

The JSON queries of the earlier lessons are called the **Query DSL**, and they are built for relevance-ranked search. ES|QL is designed for analysis instead: it runs on its own engine, which works through data in blocks, on every shard at the same time. Results without an explicit `LIMIT` stop at 1,000 rows by default.

Pass values as parameters, `?` placeholders in the query plus a `"params"` list, instead of pasting user input into the query text. As with SQL injection, pasted text could change what the query does.
concepts.code:
POST /_query?format=txt
{
  "query": "FROM orders | WHERE placed_at >= NOW() - 30 days AND status == ? | STATS revenue = SUM(total), orders = COUNT(*) BY customer.raw | SORT revenue DESC | LIMIT 3",
  "params": ["paid"]
}
#     revenue    |    orders     | customer.raw
# ---------------+---------------+---------------
# 1840.5         |12             |Ana Petrosyan
# 1290.0         |9              |Ben Sargsyan
# 977.25         |7              |Cy Hakobyan
takeaways: FROM source | command | command ... builds a table step by step
WHERE, EVAL, STATS ... BY, SORT, LIMIT cover most analysis
POST /_query; use format=txt or csv for tables
Use params instead of pasting values into the query
pitfalls: Forgetting the implicit 1,000-row limit and assuming you got the full result.

quiz.q: Which ES|QL fragment counts requests per host?
quiz.explain: STATS ... BY groups rows and computes aggregates per group.

concepts.name: Shards, replicas and cluster health
concepts.summary: Size primary shards and replicas, read green/yellow/red health, and understand how nodes share the work.
concepts.why: Shard layout decides how an index scales, survives node failures and performs, and is hard to change later.
concepts.body:
An index is divided into **primary shards**; each document lives in exactly one, chosen by **routing**: by default Elasticsearch hashes the document's `_id` (computes a number from it) to pick the shard. Each primary can have **replica** shards: full copies on other nodes, which take over if the primary's node fails and serve searches too.

- `number_of_shards` is fixed when the index is created (changing it means `_split`, `_shrink` or reindexing); the default is 1,
- `number_of_replicas` can be changed any time; the default is 1,
- a replica is never placed on the same node as its primary.

**Cluster health** summarises whether every shard has been given a node: **green** means all primaries and replicas are placed; **yellow** means all primaries are placed but some replicas aren't (a one-node cluster with replicas is always yellow); **red** means some primary isn't, so some data can't be reached. `GET _cluster/allocation/explain` tells you why a shard isn't placed.

Sizing guidance: aim for shards of roughly 10 to 50 GB, and avoid thousands of tiny shards, because every shard costs memory, open files and coordination work. More primary shards let more nodes share the writing; more replicas let more searches run at once and survive more failures, but multiply storage.

Nodes have roles: **master-eligible nodes** can manage the cluster's overall record, such as which shard is where (run three, so losing one is fine); data nodes hold shards (possibly in tiers, from fast "hot" hardware for new data to cheaper "warm" and "cold" machines for old); ingest nodes run **ingest pipelines**, steps that transform documents before they're stored; and any node can coordinate requests.
concepts.code:
PUT /logs-2026.10
{ "settings": { "number_of_shards": 3, "number_of_replicas": 1 } }

PUT /logs-2026.10/_settings
{ "number_of_replicas": 2 }

GET /_cat/shards/logs-2026.10?v&h=index,shard,prirep,state,docs,store,node
# index        shard prirep state   docs  store node
# logs-2026.10 0     p      STARTED 10231 4.1mb node-1
# logs-2026.10 0     r      STARTED 10231 4.1mb node-2
# ...

GET /_cluster/health?filter_path=status,unassigned_shards
# { "status": "yellow", "unassigned_shards": 3 }
GET /_cluster/allocation/explain
takeaways: Primary shard count is fixed at creation; replicas can change
Green: all placed; yellow: replicas missing; red: a primary missing
Aim for roughly 10-50 GB shards; avoid many tiny ones
Use three master-eligible nodes for a resilient cluster
pitfalls: Creating many indices with many shards each (oversharding), using up node memory on tiny shards.

quiz.q: A one-node cluster has an index with 1 replica. What health does it report?
quiz.explain: Replicas can't be allocated on the node holding their primary, so they stay unassigned.

concepts.name: Objects, arrays and nested fields
concepts.summary: See how lists of objects inside a document are flattened, and use the nested type and query to keep each object's fields together.
concepts.why: Searching lists of objects gives wrong matches unless you know about flattening.
concepts.body:
In JSON, a list in square brackets is an **array**, and a `{ ... }` group of fields is an **object**. Elasticsearch has no special array type: any field can hold several values. But an array of objects is flattened into multi-valued fields. A document with `"items": [ { "sku": "PEN", "qty": 1 }, { "sku": "PAD", "qty": 9 } ]` is indexed like `items.sku: [PEN, PAD]` and `items.qty: [1, 9]`. The association between a sku and its qty is lost, so a query for `sku = PEN and qty > 5` matches this document, wrongly.

The **nested** type fixes this by indexing each object as a separate hidden document tied to its parent. You then query with a `nested` query whose inner conditions must hold within one object:

```json
{ "nested": { "path": "items", "query": { "bool": { "filter": [
  { "term": { "items.sku": "PEN" } }, { "range": { "items.qty": { "gt": 5 } } } ] } } } }
```

Matching nested objects can be returned with `inner_hits`, and the `nested` and `reverse_nested` aggregations work inside them.

The costs: each nested object is an extra Lucene document (an order with 100 items is 101 documents), updating any part reindexes the whole parent, and there are limits (`index.mapping.nested_objects.limit`, 10,000 per document). Use nested only where the cross-field association matters; otherwise plain objects, or storing each item as its own document, are cheaper. The `flattened` type is another option for objects with unpredictable keys.
takeaways: Arrays of objects are flattened; which value belonged to which object is lost
nested stores each object as a hidden document
Query nested fields with the `nested` query; inner_hits shows which object matched
Nested adds documents and reindexing cost: use it deliberately
pitfalls: Querying nested fields with a normal query: it finds nothing, because nested fields need the `nested` query.

quiz.q: Why can a cart with items [{sku: PEN, qty: 1}, {sku: PAD, qty: 9}] match 'sku PEN and qty > 5' under default mapping?
options: Object arrays are flattened, so sku and qty values are no longer paired
quiz.explain: Flattening turns the array into independent multi-valued fields.

concepts.name: Aliases and zero-downtime reindexing
concepts.summary: Point applications at aliases, and switch them in one step after reindexing into a new index with a changed mapping.
concepts.why: Mappings and analyzers can't change in place, so every long-lived index eventually needs reindexing without taking search offline.
concepts.body:
An **alias** is a second name pointing at one or more indices. Applications should read and write through an alias (`products`) rather than the real index name (`products-v3`), because then you can switch the index behind it without touching the code.

The no-downtime routine when a mapping must change:

- create `products-v4` with the new mappings and settings,
- copy the data with `POST _reindex` from `products-v3` to `products-v4` (it runs as a background task; `slices` splits it into parts that run in parallel, and `wait_for_completion=false` returns at once for long jobs),
- catch up on writes that happened during the copy (have the application write to both indices meanwhile, or reindex the documents changed since the start),
- switch the alias in one `POST _aliases` request with a `remove` and an `add` action; both apply together, atomically,
- delete the old index once you're confident.

Aliases can also carry a `filter` (for example, one customer's view of a shared index) and `routing`. When an alias points at several indices, one can be marked `is_write_index` to receive the writes; this is how rollover works for indices organised by time.

`_reindex` can also transform documents on the way, with a script or an ingest pipeline, and copy from another cluster during migrations. It reads `_source`, so indices with `_source` turned off can't be reindexed.

**Index templates** (`PUT _index_template/...`) apply settings and mappings automatically to every new index whose name matches a pattern, keeping versions consistent.
takeaways: Applications use aliases, never concrete index names
Change mappings by creating a new index and _reindex
Swap aliases with one atomic _aliases request
Index templates apply mappings to new indices automatically
pitfalls: Writing real index names into the application code, which turns every reindex into a code release.

quiz.q: Why put remove and add in one _aliases request instead of two calls?
options: The swap is atomic, so the alias never points to zero or two indices
quiz.explain: All actions in one _aliases request are applied atomically.

concepts.name: Vector and hybrid search
concepts.summary: Store embeddings in dense_vector fields, run approximate nearest-neighbour (kNN) search, and combine it with keyword search.
concepts.why: Search by meaning, including finding source passages for AI assistants, relies on comparing vectors, often blended with classic text relevance.
concepts.body:
**Vector search** finds documents by meaning instead of shared words. A machine learning model turns each text into an **embedding**: a **vector**, a list of hundreds of numbers, in which texts with similar meanings get nearby numbers. The search then looks for the documents whose vectors are closest to the query's vector, so "cheap flights" can match "low-cost airfare". This is **semantic search**. Your app can compute embeddings itself, or Elasticsearch can call a model for you through an **inference endpoint** (a configured connection to such a model).

Map a field as `dense_vector` with `dims` (how many numbers) and `similarity` (how closeness is measured: `cosine`, `dot_product`, `l2_norm`, `max_inner_product`). Stored vectors are linked into an **HNSW** graph, a network joining each vector to its near neighbours, which finds close vectors fast but approximately (**kNN**, k nearest neighbours). By default the vectors are also **quantized**, stored with fewer bits per number to save memory: 8 bits (int8), or single bits (BBQ binary quantization) for long vectors in recent versions.

Query with the `knn` option or query: `k` is how many neighbours to return, `num_candidates` how many to examine per shard. More candidates find more of the true nearest neighbours (better recall) but make queries slower. Put a `filter` inside `knn` so filtering happens during the graph search rather than after it.

The `semantic_text` field type automates the whole process: it splits long text into pieces (**chunking**), creates their embeddings through an inference endpoint when documents are stored, and is queried with a simple `semantic` or `match` query.

**Hybrid search** combines word-based BM25 results with vector results. Their scores live on different scales, so use a **retriever** (a building block that produces a result list) with reciprocal rank fusion (`rrf`), which merges by position. Hybrid usually beats either method alone: words catch exact names and codes, vectors catch meaning.

Vectors need memory: keep the HNSW graph and the quantized vectors in RAM for fast queries.
takeaways: dense_vector + HNSW gives approximate kNN search
k results; num_candidates per shard trades recall for speed
semantic_text automates chunking and embedding
Combine word-based and vector results with RRF
pitfalls: Comparing raw BM25 and vector scores directly; use rank fusion instead.

quiz.q: Raising num_candidates in a kNN query mostly affects what?
options: Recall versus latency of the approximate search
quiz.explain: More candidates explored per shard improves accuracy at the cost of speed; k sets result count.

concepts.name: Lucene segments, refresh, flush and merges
concepts.summary: Learn how each shard stores an inverted index in unchangeable segments, and how refresh, the translog, flush and merging work.
concepts.why: Indexing speed, disk usage, deletes and near real-time search all follow from how Lucene stores segments.
concepts.body:
Each shard is a **Lucene** index (Lucene is the open-source search library inside Elasticsearch) made of segments. A segment is a set of files that are never changed once written, holding an **inverted index** (for each term, the list of documents and positions containing it) for text, doc values (column-by-column data) for sorting and aggregations, **points** (BKD trees) for numbers, dates and map locations, stored fields for `_source`, and vector graphs.

Write path:

- a new document is added to a **buffer** in memory and appended to the shard's **translog**, a log file that is forced onto disk (fsync) before the request is confirmed (by default, `index.translog.durability: request`),
- a refresh turns the buffer into a new searchable segment held in the operating system's file cache, without forcing it to disk; this is why search is near real-time,
- a **flush** performs a Lucene commit (forcing the segments onto disk) and trims the translog; after a crash, Elasticsearch replays the translog from the last commit.

Because segments never change, an update is a delete plus a new document, and a delete only marks the document as gone in a list of live documents. The space comes back when background **merges** combine small segments into bigger ones and drop deleted documents. Many tiny segments (from very frequent refreshes) slow searches down; merges cost disk work.

`POST /index/_forcemerge?max_num_segments=1` is useful only for indices that will never be written to again, such as yesterday's logs.

Unchangeable files are also a strength: segments stay well in the operating system's memory cache and can be read without any locking.
concepts.code:
GET /_cat/segments/products?v&h=shard,segment,docs.count,docs.deleted,size,committed,searchable
# shard segment docs.count docs.deleted size  committed searchable
# 0     _0      1000       12           310kb true      true
# 0     _1      40         0            22kb  false     true   <- refreshed, not yet flushed

POST /products/_refresh        # make recent writes searchable now
POST /products/_flush          # Lucene commit + translog trim

# read-only index: merge down to one segment, purge deleted docs
POST /logs-2026.09/_forcemerge?max_num_segments=1

GET /products/_stats/refresh,flush,merge?filter_path=**.total
takeaways: Shards are Lucene indices made of unchangeable segments
Refresh makes segments searchable; flush commits them and trims the translog
The translog keeps writes safe between commits
Updates and deletes mark old documents; merges reclaim the space
pitfalls: Force-merging an index that still receives writes, creating huge segments that are expensive to merge again.

quiz.q: Why does deleting documents not immediately reduce disk usage?
options: Segments are immutable; deleted docs are only marked until a merge rewrites the segment
Deletes are queued for a nightly job
quiz.explain: Space is reclaimed when merges drop the marked documents.

concepts.name: Distributed search: query then fetch
concepts.summary: Follow a search through the coordinating node, the query and fetch phases and routing, and see how per-shard scoring affects results.
concepts.why: Explaining slow queries, odd scores and overworked shards requires knowing how a search runs across shards.
concepts.body:
Any node receiving a search acts as the **coordinating node** for it. By default the search runs in two phases (`query_then_fetch`):

- **query phase**: the request goes to one copy (primary or replica) of every shard involved. Each shard runs the query locally and returns only the ids, sort values and scores of its own top `from + size` hits,
- the coordinating node merges these into the overall top hits,
- **fetch phase**: it then asks only the shards holding the winners for their documents (`_source`, highlights).

So a request with `from: 9990, size: 10` makes every shard return 10,000 hits to merge, which is why deep paging is costly. Aggregations are likewise computed per shard and combined on the coordinating node.

**Scoring is per shard**: IDF uses statistics from the shard, not from the whole index. With few documents, or unevenly spread data, the same document can score differently depending on its shard. `search_type=dfs_query_then_fetch` first gathers statistics from all shards, at extra cost; with enough data the difference fades.

Routing decides a document's shard: `shard = hash(_routing) % number_of_primary_shards` (internally via routing shards), with `_routing` defaulting to `_id`. Custom routing, such as by customer id when one index serves many customers, lets a search go to a single shard, but very big customers can then overload theirs (a **hot shard**).

Adaptive replica selection sends each shard request to the copy expected to answer fastest. Adding `"profile": true` to a search shows per-shard timings for each part of the query.
takeaways: The coordinating node asks every shard, merges, then fetches only the winners
Each shard returns from + size candidates: deep paging is expensive
IDF is per shard; dfs_query_then_fetch uses statistics from all shards
Custom routing targets one shard but risks hot shards
pitfalls: Diagnosing 'wrong' scores on a tiny test index with several shards: per-shard IDF differs.

quiz.q: In the query phase, what does each shard send back to the coordinator?
options: Ids, scores and sort values of its top from + size hits
quiz.explain: Full documents are fetched later, only for the global winners.

concepts.name: Data streams and lifecycle management
concepts.summary: Store time-stamped data in data streams with rollover, and manage how long it's kept and where with lifecycle policies.
concepts.why: Logs and measurements grow forever; data streams and lifecycle policies keep shards well sized and storage under control.
concepts.body:
A **data stream** is the recommended way to store data that is only ever added to and is stamped with a time, such as logs, measurements and events. You write to one name (`logs-app-default`); behind it Elasticsearch keeps hidden **backing indices** (`.ds-logs-app-default-2026.10.17-000001`...). Every document needs an `@timestamp`. Writes go to the newest backing index; searches cover all of them. Data streams accept only `create` operations, while updates and deletes go through `_update_by_query` and `_delete_by_query` or by targeting a backing index.

A data stream is created automatically on first write when a matching **index template** has `"data_stream": {}`.

**Rollover** starts a new backing index when the current one reaches a size, age or document count, keeping shards near the ideal size (for example `max_primary_shard_size: 50gb`).

Retention and tiering:

- **ILM** (index lifecycle management) policies move indices through phases: hot (rollover), warm (shrink, forcemerge, move to cheaper nodes), cold, frozen (searchable snapshots: copies kept in cheap cloud storage that can still be searched, slowly) and delete after a minimum age,
- the simpler **data stream lifecycle** sets just retention (`data_retention: "30d"`) and handles rollover automatically, a good default when you don't need tiers.

Deleting whole old backing indices is vastly cheaper than deleting documents by query, which is the core reason to organise time data this way.
concepts.code:
PUT /_ilm/policy/logs-30d
{ "policy": { "phases": {
  "hot":    { "actions": { "rollover": { "max_primary_shard_size": "50gb", "max_age": "1d" } } },
  "warm":   { "min_age": "7d",  "actions": { "forcemerge": { "max_num_segments": 1 } } },
  "delete": { "min_age": "30d", "actions": { "delete": {} } } } } }

PUT /_index_template/logs-app
{ "index_patterns": ["logs-app-*"], "data_stream": {},
  "template": { "settings": { "index.lifecycle.name": "logs-30d" },
    "mappings": { "properties": { "@timestamp": { "type": "date" },
                                  "message": { "type": "text" } } } } }

POST /logs-app-default/_doc
{ "@timestamp": "2026-10-17T09:00:00Z", "message": "user login" }
GET /_data_stream/logs-app-default
# backing index ".ds-logs-app-default-2026.10.17-000001"
takeaways: Data streams = one write name over rolling hidden backing indices
Index templates with data_stream: {} create them on first write
Rollover keeps shards sized; ILM or data stream lifecycle handles retention
Dropping old indices beats delete_by_query for time data
pitfalls: Storing years of logs in a single index and purging with delete_by_query.

quiz.q: Why is retention in data streams much cheaper than deleting old documents from one big index?
options: Whole backing indices are dropped instead of marking and merging away millions of documents
quiz.explain: Deleting an index removes its files at once, with no per-document deletes or merges.
